Regression models

Source: vignettes/regression-models.Rmd
regression-models.Rmd

A regression model of intensive longitudinal data relates an outcome on each occasion to predictors measured on the same or an earlier occasion. The data contain many occasions for each of many persons, and the model can be estimated for the sample as a whole, for groups of persons, or for each person separately (López-Pernas et al. 2025). The three levels rest on different assumptions about how far persons share the same process.

A pooled model, also termed variable-centred, estimates one set of coefficients from the data of all persons. It assumes that the coefficients are identical across persons, or that their average is the quantity of interest. When persons differ in the strength or the direction of an association, the pooled coefficient describes the average of the sample and can misdescribe most of its members (Molenaar 2004). A subgroup model, also termed person-centred, partitions the persons into groups with similar coefficients and estimates one model per group. It assumes that the heterogeneity between persons takes the form of a small number of distinct processes. A person-specific model, also termed idiographic, estimates a separate model for each person from that person’s repeated measures. It treats each person as a separate system and requires enough occasions per person to estimate the coefficients with useful precision.

Estimating the three levels on the same data turns these assumptions into testable claims. The comparison shows whether the person-specific coefficients spread more than sampling error predicts, whether that spread forms distinct groups, and how well the pooled coefficient represents the individual persons. fit_lm() estimates linear models, fit_glm() estimates generalized linear models for binary and count outcomes, and the scope argument of both selects the levels.

Linear models

The example models daily effort as a linear function of efficacy and monitoring for the 36 learners in srl. fit_lm() estimates the pooled model and one model per learner. Each model is estimated on the first 124 days of each learner, and the last 32 days are held out to evaluate predictions, as described in the prediction vignette. The pooled model combines the occasions of all learners, and occasions of the same learner are correlated, so its standard errors are clustered on the learner (Liang and Zeger 1986).

lm_fit <- fit_lm(srl, y = "effort", x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                 id = "name", time = "day",
                 scope = c("pooled", "individual"))
coefs(lm_fit, scope = "pooled")
#>    scope model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate  std_error
#> 1 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all (Intercept) 27.9366297 4.64403728
#> 2 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all    efficacy  0.4415288 0.05638120
#> 3 pooled    lm    native    .all     .all  monitoring  0.1442609 0.04962956
#>   statistic      p_value
#> 1  6.015591 7.364519e-07
#> 2  7.831136 3.341992e-09
#> 3  2.906753 6.297403e-03

In the pooled model, effort increases by 0.44 points per point of efficacy (SE = 0.056) and by 0.14 points per point of monitoring (SE = 0.050), with the other predictor held constant. These coefficients estimate the average association in the sample. The person-specific coefficients show whether this average describes the individual learners.

Person-specific coefficients

A person-specific model compares the days of one learner with each other, so its slope estimates the within-person association of that learner. The individual scope returns one slope per learner.

coefs(lm_fit, scope = "individual", term = "efficacy", sort_by = "estimate")

The person-specific efficacy slopes range from −0.18 (Ravi) to 0.87 (Lars), with a median of 0.32. Seven of the 36 learners have negative slopes, and 8 have a slope within 0.10 of the pooled value of 0.44. The observed spread of the slopes has two sources, true differences between learners and sampling error. Each slope rests on 124 days, and its standard error has a median of 0.09 across learners. The standard deviation of the observed slopes is 0.27, three times the typical standard error, so sampling error accounts for a small share of the spread.

Heterogeneity of the coefficients

The separation of true heterogeneity from sampling error is the problem that random-effects meta-analysis addresses, with persons in the role of studies (DerSimonian and Laird 1986). The model treats each person-specific slope as an estimate of that person’s true slope and the true slopes as draws from a normal distribution. It estimates the mean of the true slopes, their standard deviation τ\tau, and the share I2I^2 of the observed variance that reflects true differences. pool_coefs() applies the DerSimonian–Laird estimator to the person-specific coefficients.

pool_coefs(lm_fit)
#> POOLED PERSON EFFECTS
#>   Method   random effects (DerSimonian-Laird)
#>   People   36
#>   Terms    3
#> 
#>   term           k    pooled           95% CI   sd_obs      tau      I2      Q p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   (Intercept)   36   31.9792   [22.59, 41.37]   23.432   27.054   0.968   <1e-04
#>   efficacy      36    0.2871     [0.20, 0.38]    0.271    0.252   0.912   <1e-04
#>   monitoring    36    0.1957     [0.09, 0.30]    0.299    0.276   0.919   <1e-04
#> 
#>   sd_obs = observed spread;  tau = spread of the true coefficients
#>   I2     = share of the observed spread that is real

For efficacy, the mean of the true slopes is 0.29 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.38), τ\tau is 0.25, and I2I^2 is 0.91, so 91% of the observed variance of the slopes reflects true differences between learners. Under the normal distribution of the true slopes, 95% of learners have a slope between −0.21 and 0.78, an interval that contains learners for whom efficacy and effort are unrelated as well as learners with a strong positive association.

The mean of the true slopes, 0.29, is smaller than the pooled coefficient, 0.44, for two reasons. The pooled coefficient also contains the between-person association, which is the larger of the two for efficacy, and with the person means separated the pooled within-person slope falls to 0.37, as the section on within-person and between-person effects shows. The pooled regression also weights each learner by the within-person variance of efficacy, and learners with more variable efficacy have steeper slopes (r = 0.27), whereas the random-effects model weights each learner by the precision of that learner’s slope.

plot_coefs(lm_fit, term = "efficacy")

Figure 1. Person-specific efficacy slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the mean of the true slopes, and the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes.

Subgroups

Person-centred research assumes that the processes of many persons can be summarised by a small number of types, each type representing persons who share the same process. Effort can depend on efficacy for the learners of one type and on monitoring for the learners of another. When such types exist, a model per subgroup describes each process more faithfully than the pooled model and estimates it more precisely than the person-specific models, because each subgroup combines the occasions of several persons. The heterogeneity found above can take two forms. The slopes can form distinct clusters, which supports types, or vary continuously around a single mean, which supports a single population with individual differences in degree. Clustering methods return groups in both cases, so the form of the heterogeneity is tested before any grouping is interpreted (Bauer and Curran 2003).

test_subgroups() compares mixture models with one to four components for the person-specific slopes of efficacy and monitoring and selects the number of components by the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), on which lower values indicate a better balance of fit and complexity. A single component, the hypothesis of one population, is among the models compared.

subgroup_test <- test_subgroups(srl, y = "effort",
                                x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                                id = "name", time = "day")
subgroup_test
#> Idiographic Subgroup Test
#>   People:      36
#>   Coefficients: efficacy, monitoring
#>   Searched:    k = 1..4, covariance models EII/VII/EEI/VVI/EEE/VVV
#> 
#>   VERDICT:     no subgroups detected (one population fits best)
#>                Clustering these people anyway will still return
#>                groups -- they will not mean anything.
#> 
#>   Use as.data.frame() for the BIC table.
as.data.frame(subgroup_test) |> head()
#>   k model     loglik npar      bic selected
#> 1 1   EII -101.14942    3 213.0494     TRUE
#> 2 1   VII -101.14942    3 213.0494    FALSE
#> 3 1   EEI -101.14942    4 216.6329    FALSE
#> 4 1   VVI -101.14942    4 216.6329    FALSE
#> 5 2   EEI  -96.59769    7 218.2800    FALSE
#> 6 1   EEE -100.37905    5 218.6757    FALSE

The one-component model has the lowest BIC (213.0), and the best two-component model has a BIC of 218.3. The learners in srl therefore form a single population whose slopes differ continuously, and the person-specific models are the appropriate description of these differences.

Generalized linear models

Many outcomes of intensive longitudinal studies are binary or counts, such as whether a learner submits an assignment on a given day or how many messages a learner posts. A linear model for such outcomes predicts values outside the possible range and assumes a constant residual variance, whereas the variance of a binary or count outcome depends on its mean. A generalized linear model relates the predictors to a transformation of the expected outcome through a link function and takes the variance from the distribution of the outcome (McCullagh and Nelder 1989). For a binary outcome, the logistic model relates the predictors to the log-odds of the outcome, and a slope is the change in log-odds per unit of the predictor. fit_glm() estimates these models at the same levels as fit_lm(), with family = "binomial" for binary outcomes, "poisson" for counts, and "negbin" for counts whose variance exceeds their mean.

The submissions data are simulated, so that the true process of each learner is known and the estimates at each level can be compared with it. Forty learners are observed on 80 days, with a binary record of whether an assignment was submitted. The learners belong to two types. For the 20 engaged learners, the log-odds of submitting rise with daily motivation, with a slope of 1.2, and for the 20 avoidant learners they fall, with a slope of −0.6. The slope of each learner varies around the slope of the type with a standard deviation of 0.15, and the type column records the true type.

head(submissions)
#>   learner day    type motivation submitted
#> 1       1   1 engaged  1.3284155         1
#> 2       1   2 engaged  1.5540090         1
#> 3       1   3 engaged -0.3463324         0
#> 4       1   4 engaged  0.3191570         1
#> 5       1   5 engaged -2.3165814         0
#> 6       1   6 engaged -0.1089408         0

Pooled coefficients 

pooled_glm <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                      id = "learner", family = "binomial",
                      time = "day", scope = "pooled")
coefs(pooled_glm)
#>    scope    model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate  std_error
#> 1 pooled binomial    native    .all     .all (Intercept) -0.1210932 0.08797027
#> 2 pooled binomial    native    .all     .all  motivation  0.2297620 0.12060291
#>   statistic    p_value
#> 1 -1.376524 0.16865944
#> 2  1.905111 0.05676559

The pooled motivation slope is 0.23 (SE = 0.12, p = .057). The pooled model averages two processes of opposite sign, and its slope describes neither type. A pooled analysis of these data would conclude that motivation is at most weakly related to submission, although motivation is strongly associated with submission for every learner, positively for half of the learners and negatively for the other half.

Subgroups

The simulated data contain two types, and the subgroup analysis is expected to recover them. find_subgroups() with k = "auto" chooses the number of subgroups by the same mixture comparison as test_subgroups() and assigns the learners to subgroups by their person-specific slopes. The assignment is repeated on 30 resamples of the occasions, and the stability of the partition is the proportion of resamples in which each learner is grouped with the same learners. Stability measures the reproducibility of a partition, which is distinct from its validity, since a single continuous population divided at the same point also yields a stable partition.

set.seed(1)
submission_groups <- find_subgroups(submissions, y = "submitted",
                                    x = "motivation", id = "learner",
                                    time = "day", k = "auto", reps = 30)
submission_groups
#> Idiographic Subgroups
#>   Method:      effect_clustering
#>   Subgroups:   2 (chosen automatically)
#>   People:      40
#>   Sizes:       g1=21, g2=19
#>   Stability:   0.92 (how reproducible the partition is --
#>                NOT evidence that the subgroups are real)
#> 
#>   VERDICT:     2 subgroups (mixture BIC beats one group by 23.9: very strong evidence)
#> 
#>   Use groups(), test_subgroups(), fit_subgroups()

Two subgroups are selected, with a BIC lower by 23.9 than that of a single population, and the stability of the partition is 0.92. The partition matches the simulated types for 39 of the 40 learners. The 20 avoidant learners and 1 engaged learner form the first subgroup, and the remaining 19 engaged learners form the second. The assignment enters fit_glm() through the subgroup argument, so that the pooled, subgroup and person-specific models are estimated on the same data.

glm_fit <- fit_glm(submissions, y = "submitted", x = "motivation",
                   id = "learner", family = "binomial", time = "day",
                   scope = c("pooled", "subgroup", "individual"),
                   subgroup = submission_groups)
coefs(glm_fit, scope = "subgroup")
#>      scope    model estimator subject subgroup        term   estimate
#> 1 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g1 (Intercept) -0.2698968
#> 2 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g1  motivation -0.4353766
#> 3 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g2 (Intercept) -0.1201561
#> 4 subgroup binomial    native    .all       g2  motivation  1.1744905
#>    std_error statistic      p_value
#> 1 0.09741277 -2.770651 5.594442e-03
#> 2 0.10230837 -4.255533 2.085518e-05
#> 3 0.08109624 -1.481649 1.384338e-01
#> 4 0.06605776 17.779749 1.014329e-70

The subgroup motivation slopes are −0.44 and 1.17, against generating slopes of −0.6 and 1.2. The subgroup analysis recovers the two processes that the pooled slope averaged away. The slope of the avoidant subgroup lies closer to zero for two reasons. The person-specific slopes of the avoidant learners average −0.56, and a model fitted to the 20 avoidant learners alone gives −0.51. The engaged learner assigned to the avoidant subgroup moves the slope further toward zero.

Person-specific coefficients

The person-specific models estimate the slope of each learner from that learner’s first 64 days, with the last 16 days held out.

The person-specific slopes range from −1.38 to 1.91. They average −0.56 for the avoidant learners and 1.15 for the engaged learners, close to the generating values, so the person-specific level recovers both processes from the data of each learner alone. The cost is precision. A logistic slope estimated from 64 binary observations has a median standard error of 0.34, against 0.07 and 0.10 for the subgroup slopes, which combine the days of about 20 learners each.

Heterogeneity of the coefficients

The random-effects model of pool_coefs() summarises the person-specific slopes by a normal distribution.

pool_coefs(glm_fit)
#> POOLED PERSON EFFECTS
#>   Method   random effects (DerSimonian-Laird)
#>   People   40
#>   Terms    2
#> 
#>   term           k    pooled           95% CI   sd_obs     tau      I2       Q p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   (Intercept)   40   -0.1641   [-0.30, -0.03]    0.423   0.261   0.409   0.00446
#>   motivation    40    0.2641    [-0.04, 0.57]    0.959   0.790   0.853   < 1e-04
#> 
#>   sd_obs = observed spread;  tau = spread of the true coefficients
#>   I2     = share of the observed spread that is real

The mean of the true slopes is 0.26 (95% CI −0.04 to 0.57), τ\tau is 0.79, and I2I^2 is 0.85. The large τ\tau reflects the distance between the two types, since the slopes come from a bimodal distribution with modes near −0.6 and 1.2. The normal distribution places its mean between the two modes, at a value that describes neither type, as the pooled slope does. The test of subgroups therefore determines whether the normal summary is adequate. It suits a single population with continuous differences, as in srl, and misdescribes a population of distinct types, as in submissions.

plot_coefs(glm_fit, term = "motivation")

Figure 2. Person-specific motivation slopes with 95% confidence intervals. The dashed line marks the mean of the true slopes, and the shaded band covers the interval expected to contain 95% of the true slopes under a normal distribution.

Assumptions of the models

Each model rests on assumptions about the data. A violated assumption biases the coefficients or makes their standard errors too small.

Clustered standard errors allow the occasions of one person to be correlated with each other and assume that different persons are independent. Learners in the same classroom share the influence of their teacher, so their outcomes are correlated, and standard errors clustered on the learner then understate the uncertainty. For such designs, fit_within_between() clusters the standard errors on the classroom through its cluster argument, while fit_lm() and fit_glm() cluster on the person only.

A person-specific model is estimated from the occasions of one person, so its precision depends on the number of occasions of that person. A person with fewer than 10 complete estimation occasions receives no person-specific model, and failures() lists that person with the reason. A binary outcome carries less information per occasion than a continuous outcome, so a logistic model needs more occasions than a linear model for the same precision. A person who submits an assignment on every day, or on none, gives no information about the effect of motivation, because the outcome never varies.

The family of a generalized linear model states how the variance of the outcome relates to its mean. The binomial family applies to an outcome with two values, coded 0 and 1 or as a factor with two levels. The Poisson family applies to counts whose variance equals their mean. Counts of behaviour usually vary more than the Poisson family allows, and Poisson standard errors are then too small. The negative binomial family ("negbin") estimates this extra variance.

Comparing slopes across persons, as pool_coefs() and find_subgroups() do, assumes that every slope is measured in the same unit. This holds when every person has the same predictors, coded and transformed in the same way. Person scaling breaks it, because it divides the scores of each person by a different standard deviation, so a slope of 0.5 means a different change in raw scores for each person.

Within-person and between-person effects

A person-specific model estimates the within-person association of each person, whereas a pooled model of raw scores mixes the within-person and the between-person association. The within-between model separates the two associations in one pooled regression. Each predictor is decomposed into the person mean and the deviation from it, and both components enter the model, which therefore estimates a within-person slope and a between-person slope for each predictor (Curran and Bauer 2011; Hoffman and Stawski 2009). The difference between the two slopes is the contextual effect, the association of the person mean with the outcome beyond the association implied by the within-person slope (Mundlak 1978). The vignette on preparing panel data derives the decomposition in detail.

wb_fit <- fit_within_between(srl, y = "effort",
                             x = c("efficacy", "monitoring"),
                             id = "name", time = "day")
contextual(wb_fit)
#>   variable     within   between   contextual     S.E.            95% CI        p
#> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#>   efficacy     0.3688    0.5862       0.2174   0.1015    [0.011, 0.423]   0.0392
#>   monitoring   0.1745    0.0978      -0.0767   0.0988   [-0.277, 0.124]   0.4427
#> 
#> scope = pooled,  model = within_between,  estimator = ols,  subject = .all,  subgroup = .all

For efficacy, the within-person slope is 0.37 and the between-person slope is 0.59. The contextual effect of 0.22 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.42, p = .039) indicates that learners with a higher mean efficacy report more effort than their daily relation between efficacy and effort predicts. For monitoring, the within-person slope is 0.17 and the between-person slope is 0.10, and the contextual effect of −0.08 (95% CI −0.28 to 0.12, p = .44) is consistent with equal slopes at the two levels. With two contextual effects tested, the Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p-value for efficacy is .078 (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995), and the evidence for a contextual effect of efficacy is weak.

plot_components(wb_fit)

Figure 3. Within-person and between-person slopes with 95% confidence intervals.

Assumptions of the decomposition

The decomposition requires variation at both levels. A variable whose person means are nearly equal has no between-person component to estimate, and a variable that is constant within every person has no within-person component. variance_components(), described in the vignette on describing persons, reports the share of variance at each level.

The two slopes differ in what can bias them. The within-person slope compares occasions of the same person, so any stable characteristic of the person, measured or unmeasured, cancels from it. Variables that change from day to day and affect both predictor and outcome, such as sleep or workload, still bias it. The between-person slope compares persons, and any stable characteristic that differs between persons and affects the outcome, such as prior achievement, enters it. The contextual effect inherits this bias, so it is an association between person means and has no causal interpretation without further assumptions.

Choice of level

The level of a regression analysis follows from the research question and from the evidence about heterogeneity. A question about the average association in a population is answered by the pooled model, and the within-between model adds whether that association holds within persons, between persons, or at both levels. A question about the process of each person is answered by the person-specific models. Their coefficients are summarised by the random-effects model when they form a single population, as in srl, and by subgroup models when they form distinct types, as in submissions. The heterogeneity statistics τ\tau and I2I^2 and the test of subgroups show which of these descriptions the data support.

Person-specific coefficients estimated from short series are imprecise, and shrinkage toward the population mean improves their accuracy, as the vignette on pooling and shrinkage shows with pool_coefs() and shrink_coefs(). The prediction vignette evaluates the models on held-out occasions, and the vignette on subgroups and effects covers subgroup discovery and heterogeneous treatment effects in detail.
